title: Advanced CI/CD Architecture Patterns
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of advanced ci/cd architecture patterns and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to advanced ci/cd architecture patterns.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on advanced ci/cd architecture patterns. Advanced architectures use explicit stages, fan-out/fan-in, cross-repository events, build-once/deploy-many, and separate build privileges from production credentials. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Advanced CI/CD Architecture Patterns matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Advanced architectures use explicit stages, fan-out/fan-in, cross-repository events, build-once/deploy-many, and separate build privileges from production credentials. Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Advanced architectures use explicit stages, fan-out/fan-in, cross-repository events, build-once/deploy-many, and separate build privileges from production credentials. Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Multi-stage pipelines
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Build-once, deploy-many patterns
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

items.title: Cross-repository automation
items.text: For cross-repository automation, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Fan-out and fan-in job structures
items.text: List the supported combinations explicitly and use `include`/`exclude` or `max-parallel` to control expansion. Keep all required configurations covered and avoid unnecessary duplicate jobs.

items.title: Conditional release pipelines
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Event-driven automation
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Separating build, test, and production privileges
items.text: Use a GitHub Environment for deployment-specific secrets, variables, branch restrictions, and reviewer gates. Do not treat an environment name alone as proof that approval rules are configured.

content_blocks.code:
name: Build once, then validate artifact
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: mkdir -p dist && echo "same-artifact" > dist/build.txt
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: release-candidate
          path: dist/
  verify:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: release-candidate
      - run: test -f build.txt
content_blocks.expected_output: The verify job consumes the build job’s uploaded output instead of rebuilding it, preserving a traceable artifact flow.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository and inspect the downloaded file in the dependent job.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For real deployments, record artifact identity and permissions; do not promote an unverified build.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to advanced ci/cd architecture patterns. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain advanced ci/cd architecture patterns, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Standardize workflow behavior across teams without hiding important security boundaries.

content.task: Apply advanced ci/cd architecture patterns to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Advanced architectures use explicit stages, fan-out/fan-in, cross-repository events, build-once/deploy-many, and separate build privileges from production credentials.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Advanced architectures use explicit stages, fan-out/fan-in, cross-repository events, build-once/deploy-many, and separate build privileges from production credentials. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Advanced architectures use explicit stages, fan-out/fan-in, cross-repository events, build-once/deploy-many, and separate build privileges from production credentials.
Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery.
